source.title: A concept-aware explainability method for convolutional neural networks
source.authors: M. Gürkan; N. Arıca; F. Yarman-Vural

page_placements.theme: Multi-response units often respond to related, co-occurring or look-alike concepts

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses concept-to-filter associations to build an explainability method and reports concept similarities, but does not test whether individual neurons respond strongly to unrelated inputs or whether apparent mixtures reflect a shared feature.
record.gate_note: The paper reports concept-filter associations and overlap between filters assigned to concept pairs. These results concern filters and concept labels, not direct measurements of individual-neuron responses to unrelated inputs. Its counts of unique detectors and detecting filters measure concept/filter coverage, not polysemanticity, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a concept-filter explainability method (CAE) for ResNet18/VGG16 and evaluates it by explanation coverage, accuracy and recall. It assumes filters carry multiple concepts by design (Z=30 concepts per filter) but never measures whether individual filters respond to unrelated inputs. Its similarity scores are overlaps between top-30 filter lists for concept pairs, a different construct from single-neuron polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CAE, which allows multiple concepts per filter, outperforms NetDis, Net2Vec and CLIP-Dissect on unique detectors and detecting filters. They say it supports explanation and model comparison, while concept similarity can cause redundancy in explanations. They note a limited 200-concept dictionary and reliability problems in the segmented learning data.
record.recipe_differences: The paper estimates concept-filter associations from segmented concept regions and uses them for CNN explanations; it does not reproduce the original neuron-response examples or measure unrelated inputs.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across models and training datasets. The authors also report slight improvement when thresholding feature maps before selecting highly activated filters, but proceed without thresholding.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-30 concept-aware filter lists overlap heavily for related or co-occurring concepts (up to 93%) and partly for structurally similar ones (bird/airplane 0.27) in ResNet18/VGG16 final conv layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CNN final conv layers, concepts that co-occur or resemble each other in shape share many of their most activating filters.

record.problems: The reported similarity scores are overlaps between concept-associated filter lists, not direct neuron-response measurements or tests of whether the concepts are unrelated. The authors also state that the concept dictionary is limited and that the segmented learning data have reliability, labeling, and sample-balance concerns.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure individual-neuron responses to unrelated inputs. Tables 2–3 report concept and filter coverage, not polysemanticity; explanation accuracy and recall measure explanation performance.

untested.parts: Whether individual filters in CNN classifiers respond strongly to several unrelated inputs; only list overlaps for mostly related concept pairs are reported.
All: no superposition or capacity analysis.
All: no initialization, regularization or training-noise analysis.
Architecture effect on polysemanticity share; ResNet18 vs VGG16 is compared only on explanation metrics.
Whether mixed-response filters detect one shared feature; the bird/airplane shape remark is speculative, not tested.
Measurement dependence of polysemanticity. Thresholding was mentioned only as giving slight explanation improvement, with no polysemanticity measure.

record.verdict_notes: Multi-concept association per filter is a design choice of the method (truncation Z=30), not an empirical finding about polysemanticity. Tables 2–3 are method-performance comparisons and are correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Whether individual neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs; the paper's concept associations do not establish unrelatedness or measure neuron responses directly.
Transformer language models, MLP neurons, unrelated tokens or contexts, and layer differences.
Feature capacity pressure, sparsity, and superposition as a cause.
Initialization, regularization, training noise, or sufficient capacity for all features.
Activation functions, architecture or regularization effects on polysemanticity, including SoLU or performance costs of reducing it.
Whether individual mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots, and whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether polysemanticity depends on the activation range examined or on how neuron explanations are scored.

rows.measure: Similarity Score (shared CAF filters divided by list size)
rows.note: Measures overlap between filters assigned to two concepts; it does not show that an individual neuron responds strongly to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: List-overlap similarity between two related concepts (windowpane/blind), not a neuron's response to unrelated inputs. It is a byproduct of the method rather than a test.

relation.reason: The method assumes and uses multi-concept filters (Y=Z=30) without testing polysemanticity. 'assumes' would also fit, but the given value is acceptable.

tranche.reason: The paper builds a concept-aware explanation method that allows multiple concepts per filter by design. It reports only the method's coverage and explanation performance and never tests whether single filters respond to unrelated inputs.

source_check.notes: Similarity scores are overlaps between top-30 per-concept filter lists in the final conv layer (512 filters), not measures of a single neuron responding to unrelated inputs. Table 5's layout is scrambled in the text, but the cell order matches the four models.

statements.correction: Table 5 top pairs: windowpane/blind 93% (ResNet18-Places365) and door/door frame 90% (VGG16-ImageNet), which the authors call co-occurring/complementary; street light/traffic light 87% (VGG16-Places365) and sofa/ottoman 93% (ResNet18-ImageNet), which they attribute to resembling shapes. Bird/airplane: 8 of 30 shared CAF filters, similarity 0.27, ResNet18-ImageNet only, linked by the authors to shape resemblance ('probably').
statements.problem: The numbers are right (Y=30, final conv layer, top 93%, bird/airplane 0.27), but the split is a misreading. The authors attribute two of the top pairs to resembling shapes (street light/traffic light 87%, sofa/ottoman 93%), so structurally similar concepts are not only 'partly' overlapping. Bird/airplane is on one model only.
